new: Generative AI threatens low end; durability open. Digital Media subscriptions +11.2% y/y in Q3 FY2026 (Q1 +13.0%); Digital Experience ~13% ex-Semrush (estimated). Creative is slowing.

old: Generative AI substitutes for paid creative seats. Image and video models sold directly by model providers, and browser-first design tools such as Figma, let casual and mid-level users create without Creative Cloud. The early signal is already in the numbers: net new ARR was $400M in Q3 FY2026 against $660M a year earlier (-39%), organic ARR growth is about 9% once Semrush's ~$480M is removed, and management deferred Creative Cloud price increases. Creative and Marketing Professionals is $4.65B of the $6.56B quarterly subscription revenue (71%), so this is the core of the franchise. If revenue growth falls to 3%, the bear case gives $224.80, about today's price.
new: Generative AI substitutes paid creative seats; models and tools like Figma bypass Creative Cloud. Q3 FY2026 net new ARR $400M (-39%), organic ARR ~9%, price increases deferred. Bear case (3% growth): $224.80, about today's price.

old: Leadership turnover during a strategy change. On 1 December 2026 the CEO of 19 years hands over to Anil Chakravarthy, whose background is enterprise marketing software; the CFO left in Q2 FY2026 (interim CFO in place) and the President of Creativity and Productivity is leaving. This happens while the company switches its creative monetization from paywall-first to freemium. Narayen sold 125,000 shares (about $31.3M) on 16–17 September 2026, a week after the announcement, and now holds about $56M of stock (0.06%). A new team can reset targets, change the buyback pace or pursue a large acquisition with no track record to judge it by.
new: Leadership turnover during the shift to freemium: Chakravarthy becomes CEO 1 December 2026, CFO left Q2 FY2026, Creativity president leaving; Narayen sold ~$31.3M stock in September. An untested team could reset targets, buybacks or M&A.

old: Buybacks and M&A running ahead of free cash flow. Net debt went from -$3,762M at FY2023 to +$1,123M at Q3 FY2026 as $11.3B of FY2025 buybacks and the ~$1.56B Semrush payment exceeded FCF; Topaz Labs is pending. Leverage is still 0.11x EBITDA, so the level is not the problem. The risk is a repeat of the ~$20B Figma attempt (terminated in Q1 FY2024 with a $1B fee): a large acquisition to buy growth would cut the buyback that carries roughly 4 of the 12.9 points of annual EPS growth in the base case.
new: Buybacks and M&A outrun FCF: net debt from -$3,762M (FY2023) to +$1,123M (Q3 FY2026), still 0.11x EBITDA. Risk: a Figma-style (~$20B) deal cutting the buyback behind ~4 of 12.9 points of base-case EPS growth.

old: AI agents take the customer interface at the low end. Intuit is already plugging its software into Perplexity and Meta's Muse agent (August-September 2026), which means the agent, not TurboTax or QuickBooks, may own the first screen the customer sees. DIY is only about 12% of the TurboTax addressable market by management's own count, but it fed more than three quarters of TurboTax Live's customer additions in FY2026. If DIY units keep falling (39.9M to 39.0M in FY2026) the assisted funnel shrinks with them; the Bear case, TurboTax -3% a year and GBS ex-Mailchimp +8%, is worth $234.80 per share.
new: AI agents may own the low-end customer interface; Intuit plugs into Perplexity and Meta's Muse. DIY fed over three quarters of TurboTax Live additions; falling DIY units (39.9M to 39.0M) shrink that funnel. Bear: $234.80.

old: Credit Karma is a lead-generation business on top of lenders' appetite. It grew 20% to $2,641M in FY2026 (12% of revenue), driven by personal loans, auto insurance and cards, but revenue fell 9.5% in FY2023 when partners cut marketing. A consumer credit downturn inside the three-year window would take the segment below the 10% a year the base case assumes, and QuickBooks Capital adds balance-sheet exposure to small-business loans ($1.9B of loan volume in Q4 FY2026, though an increasing share is sold to forward-flow partners).
new: Credit Karma is lead generation on lenders' appetite: +20% to $2,641M in FY2026, but -9.5% in FY2023 when partners cut marketing. A credit downturn would miss the base case's 10%; QuickBooks Capital adds loan exposure.

old: Capital allocation and governance. Since 22 January 2026 the CEO also chairs the board, insider selling at $630-680 preceded the fall, and securities class actions allege the company misstated the effect of AI on TurboTax. None is large against a $71.6B market cap, but together they reduce the margin for trust in management's reset.
new: Capital allocation and governance: Mailchimp cost ~$12B (2021), earns ~$1.3B flat (unverified); FY2027 separation risks goodwill impairment; CEO also chairs the board; insider selling at $630-680; securities class actions over AI. Together they erode trust.

old: AI lowers the cost of writing vertical software, and the recurring base starts to leak. 75.6% of LTM revenue ($9,557M) is maintenance and recurring fees whose value rests on switching costs; if challengers or customers' own tools make switching cheaper, price increases stop sticking before customers leave. Maintenance organic growth already slowed to 2% in Q2 FY2026 (4% ex-Altera) from 5–6% historically. Each point of lost organic growth on the recurring base is about $95M of revenue a year, and at the bear case (1% maintenance, -1% total) FY2029 FCFA2S is $2,160M instead of $2,850M, C$2,225 per share instead of C$4,241. The portfolio cannot be screened for exposure from outside: management itself will not classify it by AI risk.
new: AI makes vertical software cheaper to write; the recurring base (75.6% of revenue) may leak as price increases stop sticking. Maintenance organic growth slowed to 2% in Q2 FY2026 (4% ex-Altera). Bear: C$2,225 vs C$4,241.

old: Capital allocation drifts after the founder. Mark Leonard resigned in September 2025 and left the board in May 2026; he set the hurdle-rate culture that made reinvestment work. Under Mark Miller deployment accelerated to $1,702M of total consideration in H1 FY2026, with larger deals at higher prices (DerbySoft ~$400M, bought at a multiple the CFO called high, partly with leverage) and the 2026 cohort at a 16% margin in Q2 FY2026 against the high 20s to 30s of mature cohorts. If new capital earns 12% instead of the ~20%+ implied by history, FCFA2S per share compounds at single digits and the stock deserves the bear multiple (6.5% yield). The damage would show slowly, a cohort at a time.
new: Capital allocation may drift after Mark Leonard: H1 FY2026 deployment $1,702M at higher prices (DerbySoft ~$400M); 2026 cohort margin 16% vs high 20s-30s. If new capital earns 12%, FCFA2S/share compounds at single digits (bear case).

old: Consolidated figures overstate what belongs to CSU shareholders. On top, the IRGA liability ($1,186M at Q2 FY2026, about C$79 per share) is a put held by Topicus minorities (Joday and others) that CSU may have to settle in cash; it is revalued every quarter and is not deducted in the base case. If FCFA2S is not already net of the minorities' share, attributable FCFA2S is roughly 10% lower (hypothesis) and so is the target.
new: Consolidated figures overstate CSU's share: 61.4% of Lumine, a minority economic stake in Topicus. The IRGA put ($1,186M, ~C$79/share), possibly cash-settled, is not deducted in the base case; attributable FCFA2S may be ~10% lower (hypothesis).

Management held the FY2026 target of 10.2% ending ARR growth on the $25.66B opening book, which means $28.28B at year end and about $780M of net new ARR in Q4, against $400M in Q3 and $920M in Q4 FY2025. Q4 is the seasonal enterprise quarter. Hitting it says the freemium push is costing growth only at the margin; missing it says the Q3 slowdown (-39% y/y net new ARR) is the trend.

Tiers (assume Semrush ARR flat at $480M; Q3 ARR $27.5B, rounded): Q4 net new ARR < ~$690M → FY26 organic ARR growth < 8% (claim 1 breached); < ~$440M → organic < 7% (break k1 fires). Hitting the guide (~$780M) still counts as strike 1 of k1's net-new leg (below $920M of Q4 FY2025). If Adobe discloses Semrush ARR, recompute organic with the disclosed figure.

Measurement note (k1): Adobe revalues the ARR book at new FX rates at the start of each fiscal year. The k1 net-new comparison for Q1 FY2027 against the $400M of Q1 FY2026 must use the same FX basis: restate the FY2026 figure at FY2027 rates if Adobe discloses it.
new: FY2026 10.2% ARR guide needs ~$780M Q4 net new ARR (Q3 $400M; Q4 FY2025 $920M). Below ~$690M, organic < 8% (claim 1 breached); below ~$440M, < 7% (k1 fires). Missing means slowdown is the trend.

old: Adobe trades at 13.0x LTM GAAP EPS of $17.92 and about 9.5x the FY2026 non-GAAP EPS guide of $24.45–24.50, at $233 against a $360 high in October 2025. The market is pricing generative AI as a substitute for Creative Cloud and Acrobat seats. The numbers so far show a slower franchise, not a shrinking one: revenue grew at a 10.5% 3Y CAGR to $23.8B in FY2025 and 12.9% y/y in Q3 FY2026, gross margin is 89%, GAAP operating margin is 35.7% LTM and ROIC 35%. What is slowing is the rate of new ARR: $400M net new in Q3 FY2026, down 39% y/y, while management defers price increases and pushes a freemium funnel (Creative freemium MAU >100M, +70% y/y). The thesis buys a subscription franchise at a multiple that assumes decline.
new: At $233 (13.0x LTM GAAP EPS) the market prices generative AI as a seat substitute. Numbers show a slower franchise, not a shrinking one: Q3 FY2026 revenue +12.9%, 35.7% GAAP operating margin; net new ARR fell 39%. Thesis: subscription franchise at a multiple assuming decline.

old: Valuation is 15x FY2029 GAAP EPS, not non-GAAP, so stock-based compensation (8.0% of revenue) is treated as a cost. The multiple moves from 13x to 15x, still well below the 19x of FY2025 year end; most of the return comes from EPS growth and a smaller share count. At 11x on $20 of EPS (3% growth, 32% margin) the bear case lands at $225, close to today's price.

old: The return engine is the buyback. The second leg is AI monetization inside the installed base: AI-first ending ARR above $650M (+150% y/y), Firefly ARR +40% q/q, and AEM, GenStudio and AEP each growing ARR above 20%. The engine only works if FCF holds near $10B and management does not redirect it to a large acquisition.

old: CSU is the permanent owner of about 1,300 small vertical market software businesses in 140 verticals (FY2025, FiscalAI KPIs), each selling mission-critical software to a narrow customer set: transit agencies, utilities, clubs, dealers, hospitals. 75.6% of LTM revenue ($9,557M of $12,641M) is maintenance and other recurring revenue, which grew organically 5–6% a year FX-adjusted from FY2022 to FY2025 while licences shrank. The units are not integrated; head office allocates capital and holds managers to hurdle rates. You are buying two things: an annuity of recurring fees with low churn, and a reinvestment engine that took FCFA2S from $853M in FY2022 to $1,683M in FY2025 (25% 3Y CAGR) with no new shares (21.19M since FY2021). The stock fell from C$4,993 (30 Jun 2025) to C$2,896 (29 Sep 2026) on two events: fear that AI erodes VMS pricing and switching costs, and founder Mark Leonard's resignation for health reasons in September 2025.

old: Intuit is two platforms. The business platform (Global Business Solutions: QuickBooks online and desktop, payroll, payments, capital, Mailchimp) made $12,864M in FY2026, +16%; its online ecosystem made $9,918M, +19%. The consumer platform (TurboTax $5,296M, Credit Karma $2,641M, ProTax $647M) made $8,584M, +11%. The stock fell from $683 (October 2025) to $268 because the market reads AI agents and cheap filers as the end of paid DIY tax and low-end bookkeeping. The low end is under real pressure: TurboTax federal units fell 2.3% to 39.0M and online paying customers grew only 3%. The core is not: online ecosystem ARPC grew 15%, mid-market revenue 39%, online payment volume 30% to $225B, and Credit Karma 20%. The thesis buys the ledger and tax data of millions of US small businesses and filers, plus the accountant network around them, where switching costs and compliance liability matter more than the interface.

old: The return comes from earnings growth of about 16% a year plus a share count that shrinks. In FY2026 Intuit spent $6,121M on buybacks and $1,347M on dividends out of $8,663M of FCF, and period-end shares fell 3.8%, from 279.1M to 268.4M. At today's price, a year of buybacks at that pace retires about 8% of the company. Margin support is already decided: a 17% workforce reduction announced in May 2026, and SBC guided down to 8% of revenue by FY2030. Net debt is $1,136M including leases, 0.17x EBITDA, so the buyback does not need leverage. What the thesis does not assume is a reacceleration: the new-customer push (QuickBooks Free and Lite, lower DIY tax prices) is upside if it works, and the base case already absorbs the lower tax ARPC it costs.
